iut_type: Referencing an unrelated third party's already-registered QDID without their knowledge/consent (revocation risk), and the real-world risk profile of implementing raw open-source BlueZ versus buying a certified commercial stack
customer_question: BlueZ has many existing SIG registrations from other companies -- can we just reference another (unrelated) company's already-registered Host Subsystem QDID for our own new registration?
question_variants: If using raw, unmodified open-source BlueZ as our Host Stack, what's the realistic pass rate, cost, and timeline for certification testing?
Are there commercial vendors who sell an already-certified BlueZ-based stack that can be referenced directly?
actual_issue: The customer wanted to shortcut their registration by referencing another, unrelated company's existing BlueZ-based Host Subsystem QDID (found via SIG's public registration database) rather than going through their own certification testing -- and separately needed a realistic picture of what testing raw, unmodified open-source BlueZ would actually involve.
plain_english_explanation: Referencing another, unrelated company's existing registered QDID for your own new registration is technically possible to file, but is not recommended: once filed, anyone who later searches that QDID (including the original Listing Owner) will see your company's registration appear in the results alongside theirs. If the original Listing Owner notices and objects, they can request SIG to revoke your registration, since you have no business relationship or permission from them to reference their registration. So while the filing itself might formally succeed, it carries an ongoing revocation risk that makes it inadvisable. Separately, implementing raw, unmodified open-source BlueZ as a Host Stack carries substantial real-world risk: based on past similar engagements, an as-implemented open-source BlueZ stack has historically passed only about 60% of the required intermediate-layer tests (L2CAP, GAP, SDP, BNEP/RFCOMM, SPP, etc.) on the first attempt, with the remaining 40% requiring fix-and-retest cycles (and some requiring a second round of fixes and retesting). Because these are intermediate-layer protocol tests, they require an ADB debugger setup and an on-site engineer at the test lab (in Allion's case, Taiwan) who can operate the DUT via ADB and communicate with lab engineers in English or Chinese. In one such past engagement (where the customer's Chinese subsidiary handled development and could communicate smoothly in Chinese with the Taiwan lab engineers), the full process -- including fix cycles -- took about 3 months and cost in the several-million-yen range. Some set-maker engagements have even been abandoned partway through due to this difficulty. The recommended alternative is to purchase an already-certified BlueZ-based stack from a commercial Japanese vendor/distributor, which allows legitimately referencing that vendor's own registered QDID without any revocation risk. Known vendors/distributors include Toshiba Information Systems, Ubiquitous AI Corporation (OpenSynergy's Japan distributor), Grape Systems (IVT's Japan distributor), Himiko Solutions (also an IVT distributor), Hit Corporation (Workaround GmbH's Japan distributor), and Atmark Techno (Design Gateway's Japan distributor).
consultant_answer: Technically you could file a new registration referencing another company's existing QDID, but we don't recommend it -- if that company's Listing Owner later notices your registration appearing alongside theirs in a search and you have no relationship or permission from them, they can request SIG to revoke your registration. As for raw open-source BlueZ: based on past experience, it typically passes only about 60% of required intermediate-layer tests on the first attempt, requiring fix-and-retest cycles, an ADB debugger setup, and an on-site bilingual engineer at the test lab -- in one past case this took about 3 months and cost in the several-million-yen range, and some customers have abandoned the effort partway through. We'd recommend instead purchasing an already-certified BlueZ-based stack from a commercial vendor (we can provide a list of Japanese distributors), which lets you legitimately reference their registered QDID without any revocation risk.
decision_logic: When a customer considers referencing an unrelated third party's existing registered QDID without a business relationship or permission, explain the revocation risk this creates rather than just confirming technical feasibility; and when a customer is considering implementing raw open-source BlueZ, proactively share the realistic pass-rate, cost, and timeline risk profile based on past engagements, then offer the certified-commercial-stack alternative as a lower-risk path.
final_recommendation: When a customer proposes either referencing an unrelated company's QDID or implementing raw open-source BlueZ, lead with the real-world risk profile (revocation risk for the former; pass-rate/cost/timeline risk for the latter) rather than just confirming technical feasibility, and proactively offer the certified-commercial-stack-vendor list as the lower-risk alternative.
risk_if_done_wrong: Referencing an unrelated company's QDID without permission risks a future registration revocation once noticed; committing to raw open-source BlueZ without understanding the realistic pass-rate and cost risk could result in missed production schedules or abandoned development, as has happened in past set-maker engagements.
